newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Siberians see eclipse of sun, conduct experiments.
newsitem.headline: Siberians see eclipse of sun, conduct experiments.

text.p: Scientists and curious local residents across Siberia and the Russian Far East viewed a more than two-minute long solar eclipse on Sunday that offered a rare opportunity to see a comet passing by near the sun.
Scientists from regions across Russia as well as Japan, the United States and other nations travelled to the Siberian city of Chita and elsewhere to make observations.
"It was rather strange when it became dark," said Alexander Garetov, who saw the eclipse along with a group of tourists from Japan. "It was dark and it became colder."
He said the temperature was about -20 C before the eclipse and then fell by about five degrees. He said the weather was clear and perfect for observations.
Thousands of local residents took to the streets to watch the two-minute, 18-second-long eclipse, during which the moon passed in front of the sun and brought darkness to the city.
The eclipse was seen in the Russian Far East and Siberia and small sections of northern China and Mongolia.
Several foreign tour companies brought tourists bearing special filters and cameras. Some school children from as far away as Moscow also made the long journey to the region to see the rare event.
Scientists said the eclipse offered only the third opportunity in the past 1,000 years to see a comet -- Comet Hale-Bopp -- with the naked eye during an eclipse.
John Frost, a Boston-area computer programmer who had previously seen five total eclipses, said he had planned a two-week holiday in Siberia with three other Americans around the eclipse.
Reached by telephone, he said the possibility of seeing the comet was an additional lure for him.
In the end, though he could not view the comet because of light clouds.
Itar-Tass news agency said Russian military space officials, were helping scientists study how the eclipse affected the navigation systems of satellites.
